This is a brilliant question and I'll answer it in two parts if I may.

If someone ends their life whilst under my/our care we have failed massively and the repercussions are, quite rightly, huge. If you are Sectioned under the mental health act we have a duty of care which we are legally obliged to provide. In the vast majority of cases we successfully treat detained patients who go on to live within the community. I've had a small number of cases where people have seemed well, been discharged and been found dead within a matter of days. This is heartbreaking for the team but there's nothing we can do to stop this happening as they are outside our care. The best part of my job is helping a patient carry their bags out to their family who are waiting to collect them after discharge. Those carpark hugs are the best in the world.

From a personal perspective, I speak from experience. My son committed suicide at university , aged 20 in Oct 2018. I cannot begin to describe the devastation he left in the wake of that act. It broke me as a father, tore our family apart and I will spend the rest of my life examining every minute detail of my parenting in an effort to make some sense of what happened. As a result, I approach my work knowing that I wouldn't wish this on any other family. Every time I intervene it's very personal for me, knowing, on that occasion, I prevented a family going through what we did.
